metadata.title: Computer Organization and Architecture
metadata.transferable: Transferable to both UC and CSU (C-ID: COMP-142)

meetingSchedule.time: Work on your own schedule; weekly deliverables are due Sunday 11:59 PM
meetingSchedule.location: Online through Canvas and the course learning modules
meetingSchedule.modality: Fully asynchronous online. There are no live class sessions. All content is delivered through the course's interactive learning modules, with hands-on work in Logisim and MARS. Student hours are available online each week if you want to talk something through.

description.catalog: This course will explore the organization and behavior of real computer systems at the assembly-language level. The mapping of statements and constructs in a high-level language onto sequences of machine instructions is studied, as well as the internal representation of simple data types and structures. Numerical computation is examined, noting the various data representation errors and potential procedural errors. (C-ID: COMP-142)
description.expanded:
CSC 210 is built as a single continuous progression — not a sequence of disconnected topics — running from raw voltage to a complete, working CPU simulation that you build yourself. Every new concept is introduced by naming what you can already do, surfacing the specific problem your current knowledge cannot solve, and showing the capability that closes the gap.

Starting in Phase 2, hardware and assembly language are deliberately interleaved: every instruction you write in MARS is tied to the circuit that will eventually execute it in Logisim, and every circuit you build is tied to the instruction it enables. The course ends with a CPU of your own design — one Logisim file, built from primitive gates, running a 10-instruction set you defined.

purpose.why: Most programmers never see what happens under the abstraction. This course takes the lid off. By the end you will have built, gate by gate, the machine that runs your code — registers, an ALU, RAM, a control unit, a working datapath — and written assembly that executes on it. That changes how you read every program you write afterward: you know what a variable costs, why a branch is expensive, and what the compiler is actually doing.
purpose.beyond: Beyond the hardware, this course builds a specific kind of persistence. Circuits fail silently and assembly language does exactly what you said rather than what you meant, so debugging here means forming a hypothesis, testing it, and narrowing down — the same discipline that separates working engineers from frustrated ones. The final project is also a genuine portfolio piece: a documented CPU you designed and can explain.

slos: Describe basic computer architecture, organization and design.
Discuss how fundamental high-level language constructs are implemented at the machine-language level.
Write, execute and debug small programs or segments of larger programs using an assembly language.
_sloNote: CSLOs quoted from the Course Outline of Record, as required by college syllabus policy. Expected SLO performance per the COR: 75% of students achieve each. Course objectives per the COR: demonstrate development of programs using assembly language; introduce the basic organization and operation of a digital computer at machine-language level; demonstrate how to write, execute, and debug small assembly programs or segments; demonstrate how fundamental high-level language constructs are implemented at machine-language level.

aiPolicy.title: AI Policy for This Course
aiPolicy.approach: Restricted — one sanctioned AI tool, the course AI Tutor. Other AI assistants are not permitted on graded work.
aiPolicy.scopeNote: This policy applies to CSC 210 only. Every course sets its own AI policy, and this one is deliberately narrower than most. What is permitted in another class — including other computer science classes — is not permitted here unless it is the AI Tutor.
aiPolicy.summary: This course has one approved AI tool: the CSC 210 AI Tutor, a web-based tutor introduced in Week 2. It is a frontier language model tuned specifically for this course — it knows our constraints, our tools, and where we are in the progression. Use it as much as you like. General-purpose AI assistants are not permitted on graded work in this course.
permitted: Use the AI Tutor freely, as often as you want, at any hour. It is available from Week 2 onward and there is no limit on how much you use it. Asking it for help is not a sign you are behind — it is how the tool is meant to be used.

Ask it to explain anything. Why NAND is universal, what a gated D latch is actually doing, why your ripple-carry adder is off by one, what the calling convention expects on the stack. Ask it the same question three different ways until it lands.

Ask it to help you debug your own work. Describe what your circuit does versus what you expected, or paste the assembly that is not behaving, and work through it together. Debugging with the tutor is real learning, not a shortcut.
Ask it to check your understanding before a quiz or checkpoint. Have it quiz you, or explain your design back to it and let it find the gap.
required: You build the circuits and you write the assembly. The tutor helps you understand and debug; it does not produce your deliverables. Every .circ tab and every line of MIPS you submit must be work you constructed.

Note substantial AI Tutor help when you submit. One line is enough — for example, "worked through the carry chain with the AI Tutor." This is not a penalty and never costs you points; it tells me where the course content needs to be clearer.

Be able to explain your own work. For any checkpoint or the final project, you should be able to walk me through why each part of your design is there. If you cannot explain it, it is not finished — regardless of whether it passes the test bench.
notPermitted: General-purpose AI assistants on graded work. ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, and similar tools are not permitted for the Logisim checkpoints, MIPS assignments, quizzes, exams, the research paper, or the final project.
Submitting AI-generated circuits or code as your own. A .circ file or an assembly listing that you did not build is not your work, whatever produced it.
Using AI to write the research paper. The Week 16 paper on a modern CPU feature is your reading, your synthesis, and your writing.
Sharing AI Tutor sessions as a substitute for another student's own build. Helping a classmate think is good; handing them a solution is not.
aiPolicy.whyThisLine: This is not a general suspicion of AI — it is specific to what this course does. The AI Tutor knows our constraints and general-purpose assistants do not. Ask ChatGPT how to build a register file and it will confidently hand you Logisim Evolution components, a built-in RAM block, and a multiplexer where this course requires a decoder — all of which are wrong here, and all of which will cost you a checkpoint. The tutor is tuned to Logisim Classic 2.7.1, primitive-gate construction, decoder-based selection, and the single-file build. Beyond that: two of the three CSLOs require that you write, execute, and debug the programs and describe the design. A circuit you did not build cannot demonstrate that, and the final project is where it shows.
aiPolicy.consequences: Work produced by a non-approved AI tool, or any work submitted as your own that you did not produce, falls under the College Academic Honesty Policy (AP 5500.2) and may result in a zero on the assignment, a failing grade in the course, and referral for disciplinary action. If you are behind and tempted, come to student hours instead — an extension is always available and costs you far less.
aiPolicy.uncertainty: If you are not sure whether a tool or a use is allowed, ask before you submit. Asking never counts against you. The short version: if it is the AI Tutor, yes; if it is anything else and the work is graded, no.

schedule._design: Four phases across 17 weeks, 08/17/2026 - 12/11/2026. Weekly work is due Sunday 11:59 PM unless noted. Hardware and assembly tracks interleave from Phase 2 onward. Every Logisim checkpoint adds tabs to the same single .circ file the student carries all term.

phases.title: Phase 1: Digital Foundations (Weeks 1-4)
phases.description: From binary representation to sequential logic. By the end of this phase you can build circuits that compute and circuits that remember. COR unit: data representation; computer organization (digital logic circuits). Primary CSLO: 1.

topics: Signed and unsigned representation; two's complement
Floating point and data representation error
Memory layout of arrays and records
assignments: Course orientation and tool setup: download Logisim Classic 2.7.1 and MARS
Learning module: binary and number representation (ungraded practice)
weeks.notes: Install both tools this week. Logisim Classic 2.7.1 specifically — not Logisim Evolution. Both are on the course SharePoint for Windows and macOS.

topics: AND, OR, NOT and the universality of NAND/NOR
Introduction to the course AI Tutor
assignments: Learning module: logic gates and Boolean algebra (ungraded practice)
First Logisim circuits — build from primitive gates only
Meet the AI Tutor: the course's one approved AI tool, available from this week onward
weeks.notes: The AI Tutor comes online this week. See the AI Policy under Policies & Resources for what it is and what it replaces. College deadline: last day to add, to drop without a notation, and for an enrollment-fee refund is 8/28/2026.

assignments: Learning module: combinational logic (ungraded practice)
Logisim practice builds: adder chain, decoder, comparator
weeks.notes: Decoders are used for control and addressing selection in this course; multiplexers are reserved for data-path routing. This distinction matters from here on.

assignments: Learning module: sequential logic (ungraded practice)
Quiz 1 - Digital Foundations, covering Weeks 1-4 (50 pts)
weeks.notes: Labor Day 9/7/2026 - campus holiday. This is an asynchronous course, so the week's work is unaffected; the deadline still falls on Sunday. The S-R latch is the one intentionally asynchronous circuit in the course.

phases.title: Phase 2: Assembly Language - interleaved hardware and MIPS tracks (Weeks 5-8)
phases.description: Two tracks running together. On the hardware side you build a register, an ALU, and a RAM matrix. On the software side you learn the MIPS instruction set in MARS. Each explains the other. COR units: assembly language constructs; systems programming. Primary CSLOs: 1, 2, 3.

topics: Hardware: the 8-bit register - flip-flops with load and output-enable
MIPS: the register file and register conventions
assignments: Logisim Checkpoint 1 - 8-bit register (25 pts)
MIPS Assignment 1 - first programs in MARS (35 pts)

topics: MIPS: R-type arithmetic and logic instructions
Connecting the ALU you built to the instructions you write
assignments: Logisim Checkpoint 2 - 8-bit ALU (30 pts)
MIPS Assignment 2 - arithmetic and logic (35 pts)
weeks.notes: Campus holiday 9/25/2026. Asynchronous course - the Sunday deadline is unchanged.

topics: The stack and the MIPS calling convention
assignments: MIPS Assignment 3 - control flow and procedures (40 pts)

topics: Hardware: the RAM matrix, address decoding, and the memory address register
MIPS: arrays in memory and address arithmetic
How a load instruction becomes a memory access
assignments: Logisim Checkpoint 3 - 16x16 RAM matrix with MAR (40 pts)
MIPS Assignment 4 - memory and arrays (40 pts)
Midterm Exam, covering Weeks 1-8 (150 pts)
weeks.notes: Heaviest week of the term - a checkpoint, an assignment, and the midterm. Plan ahead, and start the checkpoint early in the week.

phases.title: Phase 3: CPU Design Theory (Weeks 9-12)
phases.description: The parts become a machine. Von Neumann architecture, the fetch-decode-execute cycle, control signals, and the bus. This is where the pieces you have built start to look like a processor. COR unit: computer organization. Primary CSLOs: 1, 2.

topics: Stored-program computing and why it matters
assignments: Learning module: Von Neumann architecture and the instruction cycle (ungraded practice)

topics: Integrating the register file with the ALU
Control signals and what asserts them
Status flags: zero, carry, negative, overflow
assignments: Logisim Checkpoint 4 - register file plus ALU integration (35 pts)
CPU project plan due - your instruction set proposal and design sketch (required, feedback only)
weeks.notes: The project plan is where you define the instruction set you will implement. Getting feedback on it now is the single best predictor of a smooth final project.

assignments: Logisim Checkpoint 5 - control unit (40 pts)

topics: The memory bus and the memory data register
How the operating system gets involved
assignments: Quiz 2 - CPU Design Theory, covering Weeks 9-12 (50 pts)
weeks.notes: College deadline: last day to drop with a 'W' notation is 11/6/2026.

phases.title: Phase 4: Integration and Modern Topics (Weeks 13-17)
phases.description: Wire it all together into a working CPU, then look at what real processors do that ours does not. Ends with your complete, documented CPU simulation. COR units: assembly language constructs; systems programming. Primary CSLOs: 1, 2, 3.

topics: Complete datapath integration: PC to IR to control to ALU and register file
Implementing MOV, ADD, and SUB end to end
Timing and the clock in a full machine
Debugging a CPU that does almost the right thing
assignments: Logisim Checkpoint 6 - complete CPU executing MOV, ADD, SUB (40 pts)
weeks.notes: Veterans Day 11/11/2026 - campus holiday. Asynchronous course; the Sunday deadline is unchanged. This is the week the machine first runs a program.

topics: Wiring load and store into the datapath
Writing test programs for your own instruction set
Verification: proving your CPU does what you claim
assignments: Logisim Checkpoint 7 - full CPU with 10 or more instructions, including at least one branch/jump and one load/store (40 pts)
Instructor project feedback returned this week
weeks.notes: Checkpoint 7 is effectively the working draft of your final project. Everything after this is refinement, testing, and documentation.

topics: Clock rate, CPI, and execution time
assignments: Learning module: performance and pipelining - reading and short exercises only
weeks.deliverableDueDate: Nothing is due over the holiday
weeks.notes: THANKSGIVING WEEK 11/25-11/29/2026 - light week by design. No new Logisim work is assigned. If you are behind on Checkpoint 7, this is the week to catch up without falling further behind.

topics: Pipeline hazards and how real processors handle them
What your CPU does not do, and why real ones do
assignments: Research Paper - short paper on a modern CPU feature (100 pts)
Final project work: testing, refinement, and documentation
weeks.notes: The paper is your own reading and writing - see the AI Policy. Pick a feature your own CPU lacks and explain what problem it solves.

topics: Course synthesis: from transistor to executing program
assignments: Final Project - complete documented CPU simulation, due Friday 12/11/2026 (250 pts)
weeks.deliverableDueDate: Friday 12/11/2026 - hard deadline, grades are due
weeks.notes: Final week. Submit the single .circ file you have built all term, your instruction set documentation, and your test programs. Directly assesses all three CSLOs at once.

breakdown.description: The continuous build, one checkpoint at a time: 8-bit register (25), 8-bit ALU (30), RAM matrix (40), register file + ALU (35), control unit (40), complete CPU with MOV/ADD/SUB (40), full CPU with 10+ instructions (40). All tabs live in the single .circ file you carry all term.

Your complete, documented CPU: one Logisim file built from primitive gates, executing a self-defined instruction set of 10 or more instructions including at least one branch/jump and one memory load/store, with test programs and documentation. Due Friday 12/11/2026. Assesses all three CSLOs simultaneously.
Weeks 5-8 in MARS: first programs (35), arithmetic and logic (35), control flow and procedures (40), memory and arrays (40).
Week 8, covering Weeks 1-8: data representation, digital logic, the hardware builds through the RAM matrix, and MIPS assembly.
Quiz 1 in Week 4 covers Digital Foundations (50 pts). Quiz 2 in Week 12 covers CPU Design Theory (50 pts).
Week 16: a short paper on a modern CPU feature - cache, pipelining, out-of-order execution, multicore, or another feature your own CPU does not implement. Your reading, your synthesis, your writing.

required: Logisim Classic 2.7.1 - used for every circuit you build. Not Logisim Evolution; the two behave differently and the course is built around Classic. Free download for Windows and macOS from the course SharePoint.
MARS (MIPS Assembler and Runtime Simulator) - used for all assembly-language programming. Free.
The CSC 210 AI Tutor - the course's one approved AI tool, web-based, introduced in Week 2. Free, no account beyond your college login. See the AI Policy under Policies & Resources.
A computer capable of running Logisim and MARS (both are Java-based and run on Windows, macOS, and Linux), plus Canvas access.
No textbook purchase is required. The primary learning content is delivered through the course's own interactive modules, assignments, and Logisim/MARS activities.
optional: Primary reference (free): Saylor Academy, CS301: Computer Architecture - a free, openly licensed, self-paced online course used as this course's reference text. Its nine units map onto our four phases: Unit 3 with Phase 1, Units 2 and 4 with Phase 2, Unit 5 with Phase 3, and Units 6-8 with Phase 4. CS301 syllabus and units

Recommended: Scott, J. C., But How Do It Know? The Basic Principles of Computers for Everyone. Written for readers with no prior background, it walks step by step through the construction of a simple 8-bit computer from basic gates up to a working CPU - the same path as the 8-bit circuit builds in Weeks 5-8, so it pairs directly with the Logisim checkpoints.

Reference only, not assigned: Patterson, D. A., & Hennessy, J. L., Computer Organization and Design, MIPS Edition: The Hardware/Software Interface (Morgan Kaufmann). A second reference for the MIPS instruction set and the pipelining and performance topics in Weeks 5-7 and 15-16.

workload.breakdown: 3 hrs of learning content and lecture-equivalent modules + 6 hrs out-of-class work on Logisim builds, MIPS programming, and reading
workload.notes: This matches the Course Outline of Record: 51 in-class contact hours and 102 out-of-class hours across 17 weeks, for 153 total student learning hours. Week 8 (midterm plus a checkpoint plus an assignment) and Weeks 13-14 (CPU integration) run heavier; Week 15 is deliberately light. Circuit debugging is unpredictable by nature - start checkpoints early in the week rather than on Saturday.

policies.attendance: This is a fully asynchronous online course with no scheduled meetings, so attendance is demonstrated by regular weekly engagement: working through the learning modules, submitting deliverables, and staying in contact. Log in and make progress at least twice a week - this course builds continuously, and a week missed is not a week you can skip past, because Week 10's circuit depends on Week 5's. If you fall behind, email me early. Getting back on track is very doable in week two and very hard in week twelve.
policies.lateWork: Logisim checkpoints and MIPS assignments have a standing 48-hour grace window with no penalty and no need to ask; after that, contact me and we will work something out. Because each checkpoint feeds the next, a late checkpoint costs you more in momentum than in points - the grace window exists so a hard week does not compound. Quizzes and the midterm are open for a set window in Canvas and are not reopened afterward except for documented emergencies. The final project cannot be accepted after Friday 12/11/2026 because grades are due. This course-specific policy replaces the general late-submission statement shown under Policies & Resources.
policies.makeupExams: Makeup quizzes and a makeup midterm are available for documented emergencies. Contact me within 48 hours of the missed window. There is no final exam in this course - the final project takes its place.
policies.academicIntegrity:
See the AI Policy for This Course under Policies & Resources for the governing statement on AI in CSC 210. In short: the course AI Tutor is the one approved AI tool and you may use it as much as you like; general-purpose AI assistants are not permitted on graded work.

Beyond AI, ordinary academic honesty applies. Discussing concepts with classmates is encouraged; submitting a circuit or a program you did not build is not. Every .circ file and every line of assembly you submit must be your own construction, and you should be able to explain any part of it on request. Academic dishonesty falls under the College Academic Honesty Policy (AP 5500.2) and may result in a failing grade on the assignment or in the course, plus referral for disciplinary action. If you are unsure whether something crosses a line, ask me before you submit.
